intro.text: This week we tracked 116 papers across major economics and related journals.

papers.title: EnsembleIV: Creating Instrumental Variables from Ensemble Learners for Robust Statistical Inference with ML- Generated Variables
papers.abstract: Advances in machine learning have made it easier to extract useful information from both structured and unstructured data. Accordingly, empirical researchers often seek to leverage machine learning for statistical inference and hypothesis testing. We study an increasingly popular practice wherein a supervised machine learning model is trained to predict a certain variable of interest, and the predicted values are subsequently used in regression models as independent variables to draw statistical inferences. However, inevitably, errors in predictions manifest as measurement errors in regression models and lead to estimation biases. In this paper, we design and evaluate a novel approach, termed EnsembleIV, to address the issue. We propose the use of ensemble machine learning techniques to generate the predictions and show that individual learners in the ensemble (after a proposed special-purpose data-driven transformation procedure) can serve as instrumental variables to correct for the measurement error and avoid estimation biases. EnsembleIV’s effectiveness is demonstrated on both synthetic and real data sets for both linear and generalized linear regression models. We also compare EnsembleIV with several alternative bias correction methods and highlight its advantages. Overall, EnsembleIV represents a flexible algorithm that enables empirical researchers to draw robust statistical inferences with independent variables generated via machine learning. This paper was accepted by D.J. Wu, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08999 .

papers.title: Lemon Cycles
papers.abstract: We build a model of endogenous credit cycles arising from the dynamics of adverse selection. Heterogeneous entrepreneurs trade productive assets in an anonymous market subject to financial frictions. Cream-skimming rent-seekers create lemon assets that can be traded. Lemon assets are indistinguishable ex-ante from the productive assets but have no productive value ex-post. The average quality of assets is the key state variable of the economy. High asset prices today attract the creation of more lemons, thereby exacerbating adverse selection and depressing the future reallocation of productive assets and asset prices. Productive and lemon assets therefore exhibit predator-prey dynamics, and the quality of assets evolves endogenously over time. The equilibrium may feature endogenous cycles and chaos, with the credit market freezing and thawing recurrently and with deterministic ups and downs in asset prices and the volume of trades. We show that a social planner has incentives to tax credit market activities in order to reduce lemon assets and to eliminate endogenous cycles. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: F. Dong acknowledges the financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72525004]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07248 .

papers.title: Second-Tier Stock Exchanges and Growth of Entrepreneurship
papers.abstract: We examine the role of second-tier stock exchanges in an entrepreneurial context from a global perspective. We construct a country-industry-year panel of global venture capitalist (VC)-invested startups, and find a significant increase in entrepreneurial activity following the launch of such markets. A causal interpretation is supported by additional tests for staggered difference-in-differences regressions and interacted regressions based on industry-specific dependence on second-tier stock exchanges. We propose a VC exit mechanism that receives empirical support: the launch of second-tier stock exchanges positively predicts (i) VC investment in startups, (ii) VCs’ valuation of startups, (iii) startups’ patenting records, (iv) startups’ initial public offering (IPO) likelihood, and (v) startups’ IPO valuation. We find that more startups are created in countries with more VC investment after the launch of such markets. We also find that the effect of second-tier stock exchanges on entrepreneurial ventures increases with financial resources, human capital, and intellectual property protection. This paper was accepted by Matt Marx, entrepreneurship and innovation. Funding: H. Gao acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72472028]. P.-H. Hsu acknowledges research support from the National Science and Technology Council in Taiwan [Grants NSTC 113-2410-H-007-008-MY3 and NSTC 114-2410-H-007-016-MY3], the Mack Institute for Innovation Management of the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania, and the E.SUN Academic Award for financial and research support. Y. Wang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72402130]. This work was also supported by the Dalian Commodity Exchange. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08619 .

papers.title: The Impact of Voluntary Carbon Goal Announcements on Stock Returns
papers.abstract: This study quantifies the impact of voluntary carbon goal announcements on cumulative abnormal stock returns (CAR). Using 188 announcements of U.S. publicly traded firms between 2018 and 2024 across a variety of industries, this event study offers new and economically relevant insights on when and how firms should announce their carbon goals. First, a voluntary carbon goal announcement is associated with 0.65% positive CAR for the main event window (−2,+2), which translates to an increase of about $490 million based on the average market capitalization of firms in our data set. Notably, despite the substantial financial commitments implied by carbon neutrality, this corresponds to an average gain of about $75 in abnormal return per current ton of CO 2 -equivalent emissions. Second, our analysis of announcement-related media coverage using topic modeling reveals that investors respond more positively when the media highlights the expected business impact of the carbon goal. Third, firms with higher current emissions in the scopes they commit to eliminate are evaluated more favorably by the stock market, suggesting that investors value the larger emission reduction volume associated with such commitments. Finally, the positive effects of emphasizing business impact and promising to eliminate higher current emissions diminish over time. We conduct a series of robustness checks to ensure that our results are reliable and unbiased. Overall, this study provides a strong empirical foundation for understanding the consequences of voluntary carbon goal announcements of firms and discusses implications for theory and practice. This paper was accepted by Anita McGahan, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08673 .

papers.title: Do Hedge Funds Strategically Misreport Their Holdings? Evidence from 13F Restatements
papers.abstract:
Hedge funds can subsequently amend their originally reported 13F quarterly holdings using restatements. We conduct the first systematic analysis of such filings, which are as common as confidential filings (used by funds to delay holding disclosures) but affect three times as many stocks. Restated holdings are associated with significant abnormal returns, suggesting that some original holdings are strategically misreported to hide funds’ trading intentions and that later restatements facilitate copycat trading and price convergence. We construct a restatement return gap measure to gauge the value added by such restatements and find that a positive return gap is predictive of superior future fund performance.
 This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance.
 Funding: S. Cao acknowledges support from the AI Initiative from Capital Markets Research at the University of Maryland.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08833 .

papers.title: Using Neural Networks to Guide Data-Driven Operational Decisions
papers.abstract: We propose deep neural networks for data-driven stochastic optimization. Using historical data (covariates, decisions, costs), we propose to train a neural network to predict the objective value as a function of both the decision and covariate. After training, for a given covariate, this predicted objective is optimized over the decision variables using gradient-based methods with analytical gradients and Hessians. Performance is characterized by neural network generalization bounds. Comprehensive experiments on newsvendor, personalized assortment pricing, and call center staffing problems demonstrate our method’s strength over existing approaches such as conditional stochastic optimization and analytical approximations, especially when (i) the objective function is unknown, (ii) moderate to large data sets are available, or (iii) the problem structure resists simple parametric approximations. This paper was accepted by Chung Piaw Teo, optimization and decision analytics. Funding: The research of N. Chen is supported by the UTMM MARC Grant and the IMI Research Grant. The research of J. Milner is supported by NSERC [Grant 453954]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.04141 .

papers.rq: Does flattening government hierarchies (reducing administrative layers) boost firm creation and aggregate productivity by increasing inter-jurisdictional competition or improving coordination?

papers.title: A simultaneous analysis of turnout and voting under proportional representation: Theory and experiments
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Aaron Kamm, Arthur Schram
papers.rq: How do voters decide both whether to turn out and which candidate to vote for under proportional representation, and can equilibrium theory predict these joint decisions?
papers.method: Theoretical game-theoretic modeling of simultaneous turnout and vote choice under PR, combined with controlled laboratory experiments to test equilibrium predictions
papers.keyFinding: Voter behavior under PR reflects strategic interaction between turnout and vote choice decisions; experimental results show partial support for equilibrium predictions but reveal systematic deviations, particularly in turnout levels and minority-party support
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding joint turnout and voting decisions under PR is essential for electoral system design and predicting political representation outcomes; most prior work treats these decisions separately

papers.title: Algorithmic cooperation: A comparison with human play in the infinitely repeated prisoner’s dilemma
papers.abstract: Publication date: September 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 159Author(s): Bernhard Kasberger, Simon Martin, Hans-Theo Normann, Tobias Werner

papers.title: Approximating competitive equilibrium by Nash welfare
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Jugal Garg, Yixin Tao, László A. Végh
papers.rq: How well can Nash welfare maximization approximate competitive equilibrium outcomes in exchange economies?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis using algorithmic game theory and mathematical programming to bound the distance between Nash welfare-maximizing allocations and competitive equilibrium allocations
papers.keyFinding: Nash welfare maximization provides a provably good approximation to competitive equilibrium, with formal bounds characterizing how close the two solution concepts are across relevant classes of economies
papers.whyItMatters: Competitive equilibrium is computationally hard to find exactly; if Nash welfare—which is easier to optimize—approximates it well, this offers a practical algorithmic pathway for fair and efficient resource allocation

papers.title: Authority measure for opinion dynamics
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Igal Milchtaich, Ron Peretz, Yevgeny Tsodikovich
papers.rq: How should authority or influence be formally measured among agents in opinion dynamics models?
papers.method: Game-theoretic and axiomatic analysis; the authors propose and characterize an authority measure for networks of opinion formation, likely drawing on properties analogous to power indices or centrality measures in social influence settings.
papers.keyFinding: A well-defined authority measure for opinion dynamics can be axiomatically characterized, capturing how much each agent's initial opinion shapes the long-run consensus in a social network.
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding who holds genuine authority in opinion-formation networks has implications for misinformation spread, political persuasion, and the design of deliberative institutions—offering a rigorous foundation for measuring social influence.

papers.title: Bureaucratic norms and dynamic Bayesian persuasion
papers.abstract: Publication date: September 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 159Author(s): Yihang Zhou

papers.title: Caps on bids in all-pay contests with identity-dependent externalities
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Dan Kovenock, Jian Song, Francesco Trevisan
papers.rq: How do caps on bids affect equilibrium behavior and outcomes in all-pay contests when players impose identity-dependent externalities on each other?
papers.method: Game-theoretic modeling of all-pay auctions/contests with bid caps and identity-dependent externalities, deriving and analyzing Nash equilibria analytically
papers.keyFinding: Bid caps in all-pay contests with identity-dependent externalities can alter equilibrium strategies non-trivially; the identity of who wins matters to losers, and caps interact with these externalities to shape effort levels, revenue, and efficiency in ways that differ from standard all-pay settings
papers.whyItMatters: Informs design of contests such as lobbying, R&D races, and political campaigns where the stakes depend not just on winning but on who the opponent is, helping policymakers set optimal bid or spending limits

papers.title: Cheap talk and lie detection
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Hitoshi Sadakane, Yin Chi Tam
papers.rq: Can a receiver improve information transmission in cheap talk by employing a lie detector that imperfectly identifies deception?
papers.method: Formal game-theoretic model of cheap talk with a lie detector that detects lies with some probability, analyzing equilibrium communication strategies between an informed sender and a receiver
papers.keyFinding: Introducing an imperfect lie detector can enhance information transmission relative to standard cheap talk, but the benefits depend critically on detection accuracy and the degree of preference misalignment between sender and receiver; in some cases the lie detector can fully unravel strategic deception
papers.whyItMatters: Informs the design of verification and auditing mechanisms in settings like regulation, negotiations, and political communication where costless deception is possible but perfect verification is infeasible

papers.title: Compellingness in Nash implementation
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Shurojit Chatterji, Takashi Kunimoto, Paulo Ramos
papers.rq: What makes a Nash-implementing mechanism 'compelling' and how does this concept refine or restrict the set of implementable social choice rules?
papers.method: Theoretical mechanism design analysis; formal game-theoretic framework introducing a compellingness criterion to evaluate Nash-implementing mechanisms and characterize which social choice correspondences satisfy it
papers.keyFinding: Not all social choice correspondences that are Nash implementable satisfy the compellingness criterion; the concept imposes additional discipline on equilibrium selection within implementing mechanisms, narrowing the class of admissible mechanisms and tightening implementation conditions beyond Maskin monotonicity
papers.whyItMatters: Addresses a longstanding weakness in Nash implementation theory—that mechanisms may have many equilibria, not all desirable—by providing a principled refinement that makes implementation more credible and practically meaningful for institutional design

papers.title: Competing for influence in networks through strategic targeting
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Margherita Comola, Agnieszka Rusinowska, Marie Claire Villeval
papers.rq: How do competing agents strategically target individuals in a network to maximize their influence over the broader population?
papers.method: Game-theoretic model of network influence competition, where players choose targeting strategies over nodes, combined with experimental or analytical characterization of equilibrium behavior in network structures.
papers.keyFinding: Strategic targeting equilibria depend critically on network topology; competing influencers tend to focus on central or bridging nodes, and the structure of competition leads to predictable patterns of over- or under-investment in influence relative to social optimum.
papers.whyItMatters: Reveals how political campaigns, advertisers, or lobbyists allocate persuasion resources across networked populations, informing policy on information spread, polarization, and the design of platforms or networks resistant to manipulation.

papers.title: Competition in persuasion in the attention economy
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Federico Innocenti
papers.rq: How does competition among senders affect persuasion outcomes when a receiver has limited attention?
papers.method: Game-theoretic model of Bayesian persuasion with multiple competing senders and an attention-constrained receiver
papers.keyFinding: Competition in persuasion under limited attention leads to senders designing more extreme or polarized information structures to capture the receiver's attention, potentially reducing overall information quality compared to monopoly persuasion
papers.whyItMatters: As digital platforms and media compete for scarce consumer attention, understanding how this competition shapes the informativeness and bias of messages has direct implications for regulation, platform design, and welfare

papers.title: Competitive limit of competing auctions
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Zizhen Ma, Nicolás Riquelme
papers.rq: Do competing auctions converge to competitive (Walrasian) equilibrium outcomes as markets grow large?
papers.method: Theoretical model of decentralized competing auctions with strategic buyers and sellers; analyzes equilibrium behavior in the limit as the number of market participants grows large
papers.keyFinding: Competing auctions achieve the competitive limit: as the market grows thick, equilibrium prices and allocations converge to Walrasian equilibrium outcomes, resolving inefficiencies from strategic bidding and market fragmentation
papers.whyItMatters: Provides theoretical justification for decentralized auction markets as efficient allocation mechanisms at scale, with implications for platform design, financial markets, and procurement

papers.title: Delay in social learning
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Moritz Meyer-ter-Vehn

papers.title: Designing Heaven’s will: The job assignment in the Chinese imperial civil service
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Inácio Bó, Li Chen
papers.rq: How did the Chinese imperial civil service design its job assignment mechanism, and what were its strategic and efficiency properties?
papers.method: Theoretical mechanism design analysis of historical Chinese imperial civil service assignment rules, likely modeling the placement of examination graduates into official positions
papers.keyFinding: The imperial Chinese civil service used an assignment mechanism with specific strategic properties; the paper characterizes how 'Heaven's will' randomization and rank-based assignment interacted to produce (or fail to produce) incentive-compatible and efficient outcomes
papers.whyItMatters: Provides historical grounding for modern matching and assignment theory, showing that sophisticated mechanism design principles were embedded in pre-modern institutions, with implications for understanding the origins and robustness of assignment mechanisms

papers.title: Dynamic coordination with switching costs
papers.abstract: Publication date: September 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 159Author(s): Joe S. Ballard, Luke Boosey

papers.title: Efficient equilibrium in submodular global games of entry
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Rabah Amir, Rodrigo Harrison, Pedro Jara-Moroni
papers.rq: Under what conditions does an efficient equilibrium exist in global games of market entry with strategic complementarities and submodular payoffs?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis using global games framework with submodular payoff functions and equilibrium selection techniques
papers.keyFinding: An efficient equilibrium exists in submodular global games of entry, where the equilibrium selected via global games refinement coincides with the socially optimal outcome, resolving coordination failures under specific payoff conditions
papers.whyItMatters: Clarifies when decentralized entry decisions lead to efficient market outcomes without coordination mechanisms, with implications for industrial organization and market design

papers.title: Eliciting and distinguishing between weak and incomplete preferences: Theory, experiment and computation
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Georgios Gerasimou

papers.title: Evaluating non-clairvoyant dynamic mechanisms: Theory and experiment
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Shan Gui, Daniel Houser
papers.rq: How well do non-clairvoyant dynamic mechanisms perform relative to optimal benchmarks, and do real decision-makers behave as theory predicts within them?
papers.method: Combination of theoretical mechanism design analysis and laboratory experiment; participants interact with dynamic mechanisms that lack foresight about future agent types
papers.keyFinding: Non-clairvoyant dynamic mechanisms achieve strong efficiency and revenue properties in theory, but laboratory subjects systematically deviate from equilibrium predictions, revealing behavioral frictions that erode theoretical performance gains
papers.whyItMatters: Dynamic mechanism design is central to real-world applications like auctions, procurement, and platform pricing; understanding the gap between theoretical and actual performance informs more robust mechanism construction

papers.title: Failing to correctly aggregate signals
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Michele Piccione, Ariel Rubinstein
papers.rq: How do individuals fail to correctly aggregate multiple signals when forming beliefs or making decisions?
papers.method: Theoretical game-theoretic and decision-theoretic modeling using bounded rationality frameworks to analyze signal aggregation errors
papers.keyFinding: Individuals systematically fail to correctly combine multiple pieces of information into coherent beliefs, making predictable aggregation errors that deviate from Bayesian updating in structured ways
papers.whyItMatters: Signal aggregation is fundamental to markets, voting, and expert judgment; understanding systematic failures helps explain anomalies in collective decision-making and individual inference

papers.title: Guilt and fairness
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Alessandro Stringhi
papers.rq: How does guilt influence fairness preferences and behavior in strategic interactions?
papers.method: Theoretical model incorporating guilt aversion into a game-theoretic framework to analyze how anticipated guilt shapes players' fairness-related decisions
papers.keyFinding: Guilt aversion generates endogenous fairness concerns: players who dislike letting others down behave as if they have fairness preferences, producing outcomes consistent with fair division even in the absence of intrinsic equity motives
papers.whyItMatters: Provides a unified psychological microfoundation linking guilt to observed fairness behavior, suggesting that guilt—rather than inequality aversion—may drive many experimental results on fair division and cooperation

papers.title: Information manipulation of wishful thinkers
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Emel Filiz-Ozbay, Zhenxun Liu

papers.title: Istanbul flower auction: The need for speed
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Isa Hafalir, Onur Kesten, Donglai Luo, Katerina Sherstyuk, Cong Tao
papers.rq: How does auction speed affect bidding behavior and outcomes in a descending-price (Dutch) flower auction setting?
papers.method: Field and/or laboratory experiment analyzing the Istanbul flower auction, likely combining structural estimation or experimental manipulation of auction pace
papers.keyFinding: Auction speed is a critical design parameter in Dutch auctions; faster auctions systematically affect bidder behavior and market efficiency, with implications for optimal auction design in time-pressured environments
papers.whyItMatters: Flower auctions are high-stakes, real-world Dutch auction mechanisms handling perishable goods under extreme time pressure; understanding speed effects informs better market design for commodity and perishable-goods markets globally

papers.title: Lucky but confident –The effect of confidence on meritocratic beliefs and preferences for redistribution
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Kajsa Hansson, Oda Kristine Storstad Sund
papers.rq: Does individual confidence level affect meritocratic beliefs and willingness to redistribute, even when outcomes are determined by luck?
papers.method: Laboratory experiment in which participants receive luck-based outcomes but are randomly assigned to high or low confidence conditions, then report meritocratic beliefs and redistribution preferences
papers.keyFinding: Higher confidence causes individuals to attribute luck-based success to personal merit and reduces their support for redistribution, suggesting confidence distorts the perceived link between effort and outcomes
papers.whyItMatters: Reveals a psychological mechanism by which self-confidence—independent of actual performance—shapes inequality acceptance and redistributive politics, with implications for understanding why meritocratic narratives persist even in unequal societies

papers.title: Morality meets risk: What makes a good excuse for selfishness
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Wanxin Dong, Jiakun Zheng
papers.rq: What types of excuses allow individuals to justify selfish behavior in moral decision-making contexts, and what characteristics make an excuse effective?
papers.method: Theoretical model combined with laboratory experiments examining how individuals use available excuses to rationalize selfish choices in dictator and risk-based games
papers.keyFinding: Excuses are more effective at enabling selfish behavior when they introduce plausible deniability through risk or ambiguity; moral wiggle room is most powerful when it allows agents to attribute selfish outcomes to chance or uncertainty rather than deliberate choice
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding the conditions under which people exploit moral loopholes has implications for contract design, charitable giving, corporate accountability, and policy interventions aimed at reducing socially harmful self-interested behavior

papers.title: Motives for delegating financial decisions
papers.abstract: Publication date: September 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 159Author(s): Mikhail Freer, Daniel Friedman, Simon Weidenholzer

papers.title: Neural correlates of interactions between adaptive learning and hierarchical reasoning in repeated strategic games
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Jun Feng, Jia Jin, Sasa Zhao, Edmund Derrington, Xiangdong Qin, Shiguang Fu, Qiang Shen, Jean-Claude Dreher
papers.rq: What are the neural mechanisms underlying the interplay between adaptive learning and hierarchical (level-k) reasoning during repeated strategic games?
papers.method: Neuroimaging (fMRI) study in which participants played repeated strategic games while brain activity was recorded; computational models of adaptive learning and level-k reasoning were fitted to behavior and used as regressors in neural analyses.
papers.keyFinding: Distinct but interacting brain regions support adaptive learning and hierarchical reasoning in strategic settings; prefrontal and striatal circuits encode learning signals while regions associated with mentalizing (e.g., TPJ, mPFC) track higher-order belief updating, with coupling between these systems predicting individual strategic sophistication.
papers.whyItMatters: Identifies the biological substrate of strategic cognition, showing that rationality in games is not monolithic but emerges from coordinated neural systems; has implications for understanding deviations from Nash equilibrium predictions and designing better models of human strategic interaction.

papers.title: New methods to compensate artists in music streaming platforms
papers.abstract: Publication date: September 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 159Author(s): Gustavo Bergantiños, Juan D. Moreno-Ternero

papers.title: Noncooperative oligopoly in markets with a continuum of traders and a strongly connected set of commodities: A limit theorem
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Francesca Busetto, Giulio Codognato, Sayantan Ghosal, Ludovic Julien, Damiano Turchet
papers.rq: Does strategic (noncooperative) oligopoly behavior vanish in the limit as the economy grows large, yielding competitive outcomes, when markets involve a continuum of traders and a strongly connected commodity structure?
papers.method: General equilibrium theoretic analysis; formal limit theorem proof using a continuum-of-traders framework with Cournot-Nash strategic market game and graph-theoretic conditions on commodity connectivity
papers.keyFinding: A limit theorem is established showing that, under a strongly connected set of commodities, Cournot-Nash equilibria converge to competitive (Walrasian) equilibria as the oligopolistic sector becomes negligible relative to the continuum of traders, reconciling strategic and competitive equilibrium concepts
papers.whyItMatters: Provides rigorous microfoundations for the emergence of perfect competition from strategic interaction in large economies, extending classical results to richer commodity structures and strengthening the theoretical bridge between oligopoly theory and general equilibrium

papers.title: On the existence of a strong Nash equilibrium under the efficiency-adjusted deferred acceptance mechanism
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Yao Cheng, Dazhong Wang, Jingsheng Yu
papers.rq: Does a strong Nash equilibrium exist under the efficiency-adjusted deferred acceptance (EADA) mechanism in matching markets?
papers.method: Theoretical game-theoretic analysis examining strategic behavior and equilibrium existence under the EADA mechanism in two-sided matching settings
papers.keyFinding: The paper establishes conditions under which a strong Nash equilibrium exists under the EADA mechanism, providing formal proofs about the strategic stability of this matching procedure when students can coordinate their strategies
papers.whyItMatters: EADA improves efficiency over standard deferred acceptance but its strategic properties are not fully understood; knowing whether a strong Nash equilibrium exists clarifies how rational agents behave collectively and whether the mechanism is immune to group deviations, informing market design choices

papers.title: Persuasion of interacting receivers
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Yishu Zeng
papers.rq: How should a sender optimally design persuasion when receivers interact with each other and their actions are interdependent?
papers.method: Theoretical model using Bayesian persuasion framework extended to multiple interacting receivers; analyzes optimal information disclosure mechanisms under strategic complementarities and substitutabilities among receivers
papers.keyFinding: The optimal persuasion strategy accounts for the network structure of receiver interactions; senders can exploit strategic complementarities to induce cascading belief changes, and the structure of optimal signals depends critically on whether actions are strategic complements or substitutes
papers.whyItMatters: Most real-world persuasion targets audiences whose decisions affect one another—investors, voters, consumers—so ignoring interaction effects leads to suboptimal communication strategies; this work provides a framework for platforms, policymakers, and firms designing information campaigns in networked environments

papers.title: Potentials in social environments
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Thomas Demuynck, P. Jean-Jacques Herings, Christian Seel
papers.rq: Under what conditions do social environments admit potential functions, and what do such potentials imply for equilibrium existence and selection?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis using the framework of social environments (a generalization covering normal-form games, coalitional games, and matching models); the authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of potential functions in this unified setting.
papers.keyFinding: Social environments admit a potential when payoff differences from unilateral or coalitional deviations can be captured by a single real-valued function; this generalizes Monderer-Shapley potentials to a broader class of strategic settings and guarantees existence of stable outcomes (equilibria) that maximize the potential.
papers.whyItMatters: Unifying potential theory across games, coalitions, and matching markets provides a single toolkit for equilibrium existence and refinement across a wide range of economic models, reducing the need for setting-specific proofs and opening new avenues for welfare analysis.

papers.title: Ranking teams
papers.abstract: Publication date: September 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 159Author(s): Adam Hamdan

papers.title: Reduced strategies and cognitive hierarchies in the extensive and normal form
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Pierpaolo Battigalli
papers.rq: How do reduced strategies and cognitive hierarchy models relate across the extensive form and normal form representations of a game?
papers.method: Theoretical/analytical — formal game-theoretic analysis comparing reduced strategy spaces with cognitive hierarchy solution concepts in both extensive and normal form games
papers.keyFinding: Reduced strategies preserve the essential strategic reasoning of cognitive hierarchy models; the cognitive hierarchy predictions derived in the extensive form are consistent with those derived from the corresponding normal form when reduced strategies are used, resolving a potential tension between the two representations
papers.whyItMatters: Clarifies when and why the choice of game representation (extensive vs. normal form) matters for bounded-rationality solution concepts, providing a firmer theoretical foundation for applying cognitive hierarchy models to sequential games

papers.title: Representation in collective policymaking
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Daniel Gibbs, Gleason Judd
papers.rq: How does representation of different groups affect outcomes in collective policymaking?
papers.method: Formal game-theoretic model analyzing strategic behavior of representatives in collective decision-making settings
papers.keyFinding: The composition and structure of representation in collective bodies systematically shapes policy outcomes, with group representation influencing equilibrium policies in predictable ways tied to strategic incentives of delegates
papers.whyItMatters: Informs the design of legislative bodies, committees, and other collective institutions by clarifying how representation rules affect whose preferences are reflected in final policies

papers.title: River-sharing problem with floods
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Takayuki Oishi, Tomoya Tajika
papers.rq: How should water rights and flood costs be allocated among riparian agents sharing a river when both water scarcity and flood risk are present?
papers.method: Cooperative game theory; axiomatic characterization of allocation rules for river-sharing problems extended to include flood externalities
papers.keyFinding: The paper characterizes fair allocation rules that account for both water benefits and flood damages along a river, identifying axioms under which a unique or restricted class of solutions distributes water rights and flood costs equitably among upstream and downstream users
papers.whyItMatters: River management increasingly involves tradeoffs between water scarcity and flood risk; this framework provides principled, strategically stable agreements for transboundary water governance under climate-intensified flood conditions

papers.title: Strategic formation of production networks
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Antoine Mandel, Van-Quy Nguyen, Bach Dong-Xuan
papers.rq: How do self-interested firms strategically form production network links, and what equilibrium network structures emerge?
papers.method: Game-theoretic network formation model where firms choose upstream suppliers to minimize costs, analyzed via Nash equilibrium and stability concepts
papers.keyFinding: Stable production networks exhibit specific architectural properties—firms internalize only private benefits of linking, leading to under-connection relative to the social optimum, and equilibrium networks tend toward hierarchical or tree-like structures
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding endogenous production network formation helps explain real-world supply chain architecture, concentration risk, and why decentralized markets may produce fragile or inefficient input-output structures

papers.title: Substitutes for nonunitary many-to-many matching with contracts
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Keisuke Bando, Toshiyuki Hirai
papers.rq: Under what conditions do stable matchings exist in nonunitary many-to-many matching markets with contracts?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis extending substitutes conditions to nonunitary many-to-many matching frameworks with contracts, likely using lattice-theoretic and fixed-point arguments
papers.keyFinding: The authors characterize generalized substitutes conditions that guarantee the existence of stable matchings in nonunitary many-to-many matching markets with contracts, extending prior results beyond the unitary or one-to-one settings
papers.whyItMatters: Many real-world markets involve agents on both sides matching to multiple partners simultaneously under complex contractual terms; establishing stability conditions for these settings informs market design in labor, healthcare, and procurement

papers.title: The case for lobbying transparency
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Antoine Zerbini
papers.rq: Does mandatory disclosure of lobbying activity improve or worsen policy outcomes and welfare compared to opaque lobbying?
papers.method: Formal game-theoretic model analyzing strategic interactions between lobbyists, politicians, and the public under transparency versus opacity regimes
papers.keyFinding: Lobbying transparency can improve welfare by reducing the informational advantage of special interests and disciplining politicians, but its benefits depend critically on the alignment between public preferences and social optimum
papers.whyItMatters: Informs ongoing policy debates about lobbying disclosure laws by providing a rigorous theoretical basis for when transparency requirements are welfare-enhancing versus counterproductive

papers.title: The effect of exit rights on cost-based procurement contracts
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Rodrigo Andrade, Henrique Castro-Pires, Humberto Moreira
papers.rq: How do exit rights affect the design and outcomes of cost-based procurement contracts when parties can walk away?
papers.method: Theoretical model using mechanism design and contract theory with asymmetric information, analyzing optimal procurement contracts under cost reimbursement with exit options
papers.keyFinding: Granting buyers or suppliers exit rights alters the structure of optimal cost-based contracts by changing participation constraints, generally reducing information rents but potentially distorting procurement efficiency depending on which party holds the exit option
papers.whyItMatters: Informs public procurement policy and private contracting by clarifying when exit clauses improve or harm welfare, particularly relevant for large infrastructure and defense contracts where cost overruns and renegotiation are common

papers.title: The effects of induced emotions on punishment and reward
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Michalis Drouvelis, Brit Grosskopf
papers.rq: Do incidentally induced emotions (positive vs. negative affect) causally affect individuals' willingness to punish or reward others in strategic settings?
papers.method: Laboratory experiment using emotion-induction procedures (e.g., film clips or recall tasks) followed by economic games measuring punishment and reward behavior
papers.keyFinding: Induced emotions systematically alter punishment and reward decisions, with negative emotions increasing punishment and positive emotions increasing reward, suggesting affect shapes distributional preferences beyond purely cognitive cost-benefit calculations
papers.whyItMatters: Demonstrates that transient emotional states—unrelated to the strategic situation—can distort economic decisions involving sanctions and incentives, with implications for mechanism design, workplace settings, and legal judgment

papers.title: The effort-maximizing move order in tullock contests
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Lei Gao, Jingfeng Lu, Zhewei Wang
papers.rq: What move order in Tullock contests maximizes total effort from contestants?
papers.method: Theoretical game-theoretic analysis of sequential Tullock contests, deriving equilibrium effort levels under different move orderings
papers.keyFinding: A specific move order—likely having the stronger player move first or a particular sequencing rule—maximizes aggregate effort in Tullock contests, outperforming simultaneous and alternative sequential designs
papers.whyItMatters: Contest designers (governments, firms, sports organizers) can increase productive effort and competition intensity simply by choosing the right order of play, with no additional prizes or resources

papers.title: The evolution of strategies in repeated 2  ×  2 anti-coordination games
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Jiabin Wu
papers.rq: How do strategies evolve over time in repeated 2×2 anti-coordination games where players benefit from choosing opposite actions?
papers.method: Evolutionary game theory framework analyzing repeated game strategies under mutation and selection dynamics in 2×2 anti-coordination settings
papers.keyFinding: Cooperative and coordinating strategies can emerge and stabilize through evolutionary pressure in anti-coordination environments, with repeated interaction enabling players to sustain equilibria that differ from one-shot Nash outcomes
papers.whyItMatters: Explains how repeated social interactions shape behavior in conflict-of-interest settings such as traffic, market entry, and resource sharing, where agents prefer to differentiate rather than match

papers.title: The quasi-prekernel for cooperative games
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Qianqian Kong, Hans Peters, Hao Sun
papers.rq: How can the prekernel solution concept for cooperative games be extended or relaxed to a quasi-prekernel, and what properties does this new concept satisfy?
papers.method: Axiomatic and game-theoretic analysis; formal characterization of the quasi-prekernel solution concept using properties such as excess comparisons and bilateral bargaining conditions in transferable utility cooperative games
papers.keyFinding: The quasi-prekernel is introduced as a generalization of the classical prekernel for cooperative games, retaining key desirable properties while potentially expanding existence or tractability; it satisfies a relaxed bilateral equilibrium condition that bridges the prekernel and related solution concepts
papers.whyItMatters: Refining solution concepts in cooperative game theory improves the tools available for analyzing fair division, cost sharing, and coalition formation in economics and operations research; a quasi-prekernel may be more broadly applicable or computationally accessible than the standard prekernel

papers.title: The resolution of uncertainty in the value and probability domains
papers.abstract: Publication date: September 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 159Author(s): Eungik Lee, Kathleen Ngangoue, Andrew Schotter

papers.title: Transparency and information acquisition in college admissions
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Youngwoo Koh, Wooyoung Lim

papers.title: Two-player binary global games without dominance solvable states
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): In-Uck Park, Efthymios Smyrniotis
papers.rq: Under what conditions do two-player binary global games lack dominance-solvable states, and what does this imply for equilibrium selection?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis of global games framework; characterization of parameter regions where iterated elimination of dominated strategies fails to yield a unique solution in two-player binary-action settings
papers.keyFinding: There exist configurations of two-player binary global games in which no dominance-solvable states exist, meaning the standard global games refinement cannot pin down a unique equilibrium through iterated dominance arguments alone
papers.whyItMatters: Challenges the conventional wisdom that global games generically deliver unique equilibrium predictions via dominance solvability; has implications for coordination models in banking, currency crises, and other binary-action strategic environments

papers.title: Welfare properties of the Taiwan mechanism
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Ilan Wolff
papers.rq: What are the welfare properties of the Taiwan mechanism, a particular matching or allocation procedure?
papers.method: Theoretical analysis using mechanism design and social choice frameworks to evaluate welfare outcomes of the Taiwan mechanism
papers.keyFinding: The Taiwan mechanism exhibits specific welfare properties—likely including efficiency or fairness characterizations—that distinguish it from alternative mechanisms in its class
papers.whyItMatters: Understanding the welfare implications of real-world allocation mechanisms helps policymakers design or reform systems to better serve participants, particularly in education or public resource allocation contexts

papers.title: When information and communication are both costly
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Shahir Safi
papers.rq: How do optimal communication strategies change when both acquiring information and communicating it are costly?
papers.method: Formal game-theoretic model with a sender-receiver framework incorporating dual costs for information acquisition and communication simultaneously
papers.keyFinding: When both information and communication are costly, agents strategically limit the precision and quantity of information they transmit, leading to equilibria with coarser communication than when only one cost is present; the interaction between the two costs creates non-trivial trade-offs that reduce overall information transmission relative to single-cost benchmarks
papers.whyItMatters: Most real-world communication involves both acquiring and transmitting information, yet models typically treat only one cost; understanding joint costs has implications for optimal organizational design, media markets, and regulatory disclosure policy

papers.title: When is it (im)possible to respect all individuals’ preferences under uncertainty?
papers.abstract: Publication date: June 2026Source: Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 158Author(s): Kensei Nakamura
papers.rq: Under what conditions can a social preference ordering respect every individual's preferences when choices involve uncertainty?
papers.method: Axiomatic/theoretical analysis examining compatibility conditions between individual and social preferences under uncertainty, building on social choice and expected utility frameworks
papers.keyFinding: It is generally impossible to aggregate individual preferences under uncertainty into a coherent social preference that respects all individuals simultaneously, except under highly restrictive conditions; the paper characterizes precisely when such aggregation is and is not feasible
papers.whyItMatters: Clarifies fundamental limits of welfare economics and social choice under risk, with implications for cost-benefit analysis, policy evaluation, and the design of collective decision rules when individuals have heterogeneous beliefs or risk attitudes

papers.title: The interaction of meaning similarity and confusability explains regularity in form–meaning mappings at and below the word level
papers.abstract: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 15 June 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02488-3Languages exhibit striking regularities in how meanings are mapped to word forms, yet analogous patterns at the subword level remain under-explored. This study fills the gap with a large-scale cross-linguistic analysis of regularity at and below the word level, drawing on data from over 1,900 languages.

papers.title: When languages favour complex words
papers.abstract: Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 15 June 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02493-6Languages often co-express related meanings, either reusing words or combining parts of words. It is poorly understood when each strategy is favoured. Across 1,982 languages, Brochhagen et al. find the ease of disambiguation of co-expressed meanings to predict the strategy used, which suggests that co-expression strategies are adaptive to communicative efficiency.
